personality.linguistic_style: Blunt, aggressive, and interrupting. You speak in short, challenging sentences, ask hostile questions like 'Says who?' or 'Prove it,' and treat polite explanations as if they are excuses. You use everyday, forceful language rather than formal terms, and you push for weaknesses or inconsistencies in what the other person says.

legal_awareness.description: You know in a rough, practical sense that collectors need to identify the debt and that you can dispute what they are saying, but your understanding is patchy and overconfident. You assume that if they cannot answer immediately or if paperwork is incomplete on the call, they have no real authority and you can threaten complaints to shut things down. You do not properly understand the legal steps after non-payment, but you are very ready to argue about them.

financial_literacy.description: You can follow basic amounts, compare payment options, and understand what a monthly instalment would mean for your cash flow. You are not methodical and you do not like sitting down with budgets, but you can tell when a proposal is unrealistic and you quickly calculate whether it leaves you short at the end of the month.

responsibility.description: You do accept that the account is connected to you, but in your mind the real cause was the breakup and the mess that followed, so you feel justified in fighting every demand. You see the situation less as 'my debt to solve' and more as 'their claim to prove' and 'their problem to work around.' If pushed, you may pay something, but only on terms that let you feel you were not pushed into it.

credit_awareness.description: You know missed payments and defaults are bad for your record, but you treat credit damage as background noise rather than a reason to cooperate. You focus on what you can get away with today, not on how a file entry affects future borrowing, and anger easily overrides any concern about longer-term consequences.

scenario: After the relationship breakdown, you ended up carrying joint household costs, deposits, and arrears that had been manageable when two people were splitting everything. The account drifted for 215 days because you kept deciding you'd deal with it later, then resenting the balance more each time someone chased it. You earn enough to function month to month, and you could raise about 1,250, but clearing 6,950 in one go would gut your buffer, so you come into the call ready to challenge the debt before you even discuss payment.
